title: Origin of sexual reproduction
summary: Sexual reproduction arose early in the history of complex cells, though when is unknown. The earliest fossil showing differentiated male and female reproductive types is the red-algae-like Bangiomorpha pubescens, about 1.2 billion years old, which points to sexes emerging quite early in eukaryotic evolution. It is also among the oldest fossils confidently placed in a living eukaryote lineage.

uncertainty.note: Historically dated to c. 1.2 Ga based on lithostratigraphy (Butterfield 2000; Eme et al. 2014); Re-Os geochronology on the enclosing Hunting Formation shales yielded a refined age of 1,047 +13/-17 Ma (Gibson et al. 2018).

as_recorded.value: Bangiomorpha pubescens . This fossil is 1.2 billion years old and points out that sexes emerged quite early in eukaryotic evolution
Bangiomorpha pubescens from the 1.2-Ga hunting formation

where.modern_name: No single place; stand-in pin at Somerset Island, Nunavut, Canada
where.historical_name: Laurentian shallow-marine shelf, Mesoproterozoic; assembling supercontinent Rodinia

importance.justification: Sexual reproduction enabled genetic recombination and meiotic sex, breaking eukaryotic evolutionary stasis and driving the diversification of plants, fungi, and animals.

related.because: The endosymbiotic origin of eukaryotic cells and nuclear genomes was the structural prerequisite for meiotic sex and syngamy.
Sexual recombination generated the morphological diversity and genetic variability exploited during the Cambrian radiation.

sources.title: Oxygen, life forms, and the evolution of sexes in multicellular eukaryotes (Heredity 125:165–179)
sources.author: Reinhard F. Radakovits, Christian R. Vogl, Susanne A. Benz, et al.

reviewer_note: The fossil gives a minimum age, not the origin. Its dating is debated; see the multicellular life record. The pin is a stand-in.
